framework: AP Microeconomics Course and Exam Description (effective fall 2026)
subject: Microeconomics

source.licence: © College Board; structure + our own wording only

outcomes.text: Define resources and explain what causes them to be scarce.
Explain that trade-offs arise because resources cannot meet all wants and needs.
Note most factors of production are scarce, but non-rival knowledge may not be.
Define how the economic system shapes resource allocation.
State the three allocation questions: what, how and for whom to produce.
Compare command, market and mixed economies as ways to allocate scarce resources.
Define and graph the PPC, explain what it shows, and calculate opportunity cost from it.
Explain the PPC as a model of trade-offs in allocating resources.
Use the PPC to show scarcity, opportunity cost, efficiency, idle resources and growth.
Relate the PPC's shape to constant, increasing or decreasing opportunity costs.
Explain PPC shifts from changes in factors of production, productivity or technology.
Explain that economic growth shifts the PPC outward.
Define and determine absolute and comparative advantage from PPCs or tables.
Define absolute advantage as producing more with the same resources.
Define comparative advantage as producing at a lower opportunity cost.
Explain gains from specialization and calculate mutually beneficial terms of trade.
Explain that specializing by comparative advantage lets consumption go beyond the PPC.
Explain that opportunity costs set the range of terms of trade that benefit both sides.
Define, explain and calculate the opportunity cost of choices.
Explain rational agents count implicit and explicit opportunity costs in total economic cost.
Explain total benefits are utility for consumers and total revenue for firms.
Explain and calculate a decision by comparing total benefits and total costs.
Explain net benefit, benefits minus costs, is maximized at the optimal choice.
Tell decisions that can use marginal analysis from those needing total comparison.
Define consumer-choice assumptions and explain and calculate decisions using marginal benefit and cost.
Explain that consumers decide optimally under constraints.
Explain the model assumes consumers maximize total utility.
Explain diminishing marginal utility.
Allocate income by equating marginal utility per dollar across goods.
Define marginal analysis and use it to explain decisions with tables or graphs.
Compare marginal benefit with marginal cost to raise, lower or keep an activity level.
Explain the optimal quantity ignores sunk costs and fixed benefits from past choices.
Explain the optimum is where marginal benefit equals marginal cost or total benefit peaks.
Define demand terms and explain how price changes quantity demanded under incentives and constraints.
Explain a clear system of property rights is needed for markets to work well.
Explain that economic agents respond to incentives.
Explain that people respond to prices but face limits like income, time and regulation.
State the law of demand: own-price changes move quantity demanded the opposite way along the curve.
Explain the downward slope via income effect, substitution effect and diminishing marginal utility.
Build market demand by summing individual demand curves.
Explain how changes in demand determinants shift the demand curve.
Show that changes in determinants of demand shift the curve.
Define the law of supply and explain the price and quantity supplied link.
Explain that own-price changes move quantity supplied the same way along the supply curve.
Build market supply by summing individual supply and see it slopes upward.
Explain how producers respond to changes in incentives and technology.
Show that changes in determinants of supply shift the curve.
Define, explain and calculate elasticity measures and how price changes affect total revenue.
Describe elasticity as the size of the percentage quantity response to own-price, income and related-price changes.
Calculate price elasticity of demand as percent change in quantity over percent change in price; slope is not elasticity.
Classify demand as elastic, inelastic or unit elastic using a magnitude of 1.
Name factors such as substitutes that affect price elasticity of demand.
Predict how a price change affects total revenue given the elasticity type.
Calculate price elasticity of supply as percent change in quantity supplied over percent change in price.
Classify supply as elastic, inelastic or unit elastic using a magnitude of 1.
Name factors such as alternative input prices that affect supply elasticity.
Recognize elasticity can be measured for any determinant of demand or supply.
Use income elasticity of demand to tell normal from inferior goods.
Use cross-price elasticity to tell substitutes, complements or unrelated goods.

topics.title: 2.6 Market Equilibrium and Consumer and Producer Surplus

outcomes.text: Define and calculate equilibrium, consumer surplus and producer surplus from graphs or tables.
Use supply and demand to explain what drives prices and quantities across markets and time.
Explain that in perfect competition the price clears the market with no shortage or surplus.
Explain that equilibrium price guides resource allocation.
Use consumer and producer surplus to measure market benefits and efficiency.
Explain equilibrium maximizes total surplus absent market failures, so competitive markets are efficient.

topics.title: 2.7 Market Disequilibrium and Changes in Equilibrium

outcomes.text: Define surplus and shortage, and explain and calculate effects of shocks on price, quantity and surplus.
Explain that shortages and surpluses push price and quantity toward equilibrium.
Explain that supply or demand shifts change price, quantity and surplus, depending on elasticities.

topics.title: 2.8 The Effects of Government Intervention in Markets

outcomes.text: Define government price and quantity interventions and explain and calculate their market effects.
Explain price floors, ceilings and quantity regulations change incentives and outcomes.
Explain taxes and subsidies shift supply and demand curves.
Note taxes and subsidies change government revenues or costs.
Explain intervention in an already efficient market can only lower allocative efficiency.
Define deadweight loss as buyers' and sellers' losses from intervention.
Explain tax and subsidy incidence depends on supply and demand elasticity.
Define tariffs and quotas and explain and calculate how they change market outcomes.
Explain how opening to trade changes price, surplus and total surplus compared with autarky.
Explain tariffs' effects on price, quantity, government revenue and surplus.
Explain quotas' effects on quantity, price and surplus.

units.title: Unit 3: Production, Cost, and the Perfect Competition Model

outcomes.text: Define production and cost terms, explain how they relate in short and long run, and calculate productivity and costs.
Explain the production function links inputs to outputs in short and long run.
Explain how marginal and average product change with input use, and total product with them.
Explain diminishing marginal returns when one input rises with others fixed.
Explain fixed plus variable costs make total cost.
Describe how marginal, average and variable costs change with output while total fixed cost stays constant.
Explain diminishing returns give an upward-sloping marginal cost curve.
Explain specialization and division of labor lower marginal cost.
Explain cost curves shift with input costs and productivity.
Explain that in the long run all inputs adjust, so all costs are variable.
Describe increasing, decreasing and constant returns to scale.
Describe economies, diseconomies and constant returns to scale on long-run average total cost.
Explain minimum efficient scale shapes firm concentration and market structure.
Define profit types, explain firm responses to profit, and calculate profit or loss.
Explain firms respond to economic profit or loss, not accounting profit.
Explain accounting profit omits implicit costs; covering them gives normal profit.
Define and explain the profit-maximizing rule and output level.
Explain firms maximize profit by comparing marginal revenue with marginal cost.

topics.title: 3.6 Firms' Short-Run Decisions to Produce and Long-Run Decisions to Enter or Exit a Market

outcomes.text: Explain short-run produce-or-shut-down decisions and long-run entry and exit.
Decide to operate or shut down by comparing total revenue to variable cost, or price to AVC.
Explain with free entry and exit, firms enter for profits and exit when expecting losses.
Define perfect competition and efficiency, explain equilibrium and firm decisions, and calculate profit or loss.
State that perfect competition is efficient: no barriers to entry and no market power.
Explain prices signal marginal costs and benefits, so price equals marginal cost when efficient.
Explain competitive firms sell all output at the market price.
Explain price-taking firms produce where marginal cost equals marginal revenue.
Explain price equals marginal benefit and marginal cost, giving allocative efficiency.
Explain short-run profits or losses lead to entry or exit toward long-run equilibrium.
Describe long-run equilibrium: efficient scale, price equals MC and minimum ATC, zero economic profit.
Distinguish constant, increasing and decreasing cost industries and their long-run prices.
State long-run perfect competition is allocatively and productively efficient.
Define imperfect competition and explain equilibrium, surplus, profit and deadweight loss, and why prices fail to coordinate efficiently.
List monopoly, oligopoly and monopolistic competition in product markets and monopsony in factor markets.
Explain an imperfect competitor must lower price to sell more units.
Explain that price exceeds marginal cost and marginal benefit in inefficient markets.
Explain barriers to entry (start-up costs, law, key resource ownership) sustain imperfect markets.
Explain a monopoly exists because of barriers to entry.
Find monopoly output where MR equals MC, with price above marginal cost.
Describe a natural monopoly as one with economies of scale across all demand.
Explain how a firm with market power uses price discrimination to raise profit or capture surplus.
Explain perfect price discrimination: output where price equals MC, all surplus captured, no deadweight loss.
Explain short-run profit patterns, advertising, zero long-run profit, excess capacity and allocative inefficiency.
Define oligopoly and game terms and explain and calculate strategies and equilibria in simple games.
Describe oligopoly as inefficient, with few interdependent firms and high entry barriers.
Explain oligopolists have an incentive to collude and form cartels.
Define a game as actions whose payoffs depend on one's own and others' choices.
Define a strategy and read a normal-form payoff table.
Identify a dominant strategy as the always-better action regardless of the other player.
Define a Nash equilibrium where no player gains by changing action alone.
Explain why oligopolists struggle to reach the monopoly outcome, like the Prisoner's Dilemma, yet prices stay higher than in perfect competition.
Define factor-market terms, explain links among factors, firms and factor prices, and calculate MRP and marginal resource cost.
Explain factors respond to wages, interest and rent, and hiring depends on productivity, output price and factor cost.
Explain labor demand falls and labor supply rises with the wage.

topics.title: 5.2 Changes in Factor Demand and Factor Supply

outcomes.text: Explain firm and factor responses to changes in incentives and constraints.
Name labor-demand determinants such as output price and worker productivity that shift demand.
Name labor-supply determinants such as immigration, education, conditions and preferences that shift supply.

topics.title: 5.3 Profit-Maximizing Behavior in Perfectly Competitive Factor Markets

outcomes.text: Define competitive factor markets and explain and calculate profit-maximizing labor hiring.
Explain firms hire where wage equals marginal revenue product of labor.
Explain firms hire while MRP of labor exceeds the market wage.
Explain firms equalize marginal product per dollar across inputs to minimize cost.
Define MRP = MP x MR and VMPL = MPL x P for competitive output markets.
Define monopsony and explain and calculate its profit-maximizing hiring.
Explain a monopsonist hires while MRP exceeds marginal factor cost.
Explain marginal factor cost exceeds the labor supply price for a monopsonist.

units.title: Unit 6: Market Failure and the Role of Government

topics.title: 6.1 Socially Efficient and Inefficient Market Outcomes

outcomes.text: Define social efficiency and explain why perfectly competitive allocation is socially efficient.
Explain the optimal quantity is where marginal benefit equals marginal cost, maximizing total surplus.
Explain market quantity is socially optimal only when social costs and benefits are internalized.
Explain how private incentives can cause socially inefficient outcomes.
Explain rational agents can exploit market power.
Explain equating private marginal benefit and cost can cause market inefficiency.
Explain policymakers use cost-benefit analysis to weigh actions against inefficiency.
Explain policies equating marginal social benefit and cost can remove inefficiency.
Explain imperfect-market allocations versus efficient ones and calculate deadweight loss.
Name causes of inefficient equilibria: market power, externalities, asymmetric information, too few public goods.
Explain any non-efficient quantity creates deadweight loss.
Define externalities and explain why private markets ignore social costs and benefits.
Explain the social optimum is where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost.
Describe positive and negative externalities arising from unclear property rights or high transaction costs.
Explain agents respond to private, not external, costs and benefits.
Explain the incentive to free ride when a good is non-excludable.
Explain how public policy addresses positive and negative externalities.
List policies: taxes, subsidies, regulation, public provision and property rights assignment.
Classify goods as rival and/or excludable and explain how this shapes behavior.
Define private goods as rival and excludable, public goods as non-rival and non-excludable.
Explain the free rider problem leaves government to produce public goods.
Note governments sometimes provide private goods like education freely.
Explain open-access resources, rival but non-excludable, get overconsumed.

topics.title: 6.4 The Effects of Government Intervention in Different Market Structures

outcomes.text: Define policy interventions in imperfect markets and explain and calculate their effects.
Explain per-unit taxes and subsidies affect prices, quantity, surplus, deadweight loss and revenue, depending on elasticity.
Explain lump-sum taxes and subsidies change only fixed costs.
Explain binding price ceilings and floors act differently across market structures.
Explain intervention can raise efficiency if it fixes the incentives behind the failure.
Explain price regulation can address monopoly inefficiency.
Explain a natural monopoly needs a lump-sum subsidy to produce the efficient quantity.
Explain antitrust policy aims to make markets more competitive.
Define measures of income and wealth inequality.
Note income and poverty rates vary across and within groups and countries.
Explain the Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient represent and compare inequality.
Explain sources of income and wealth inequality.
Explain factors earning their marginal product can contribute to inequality.
List sources: tax structures, human and social capital, inheritance, discrimination, finance access, mobility, bargaining power.
